title: The benefits of good posture
speaker: Murat Dalkilinç (narrated by Addison Anderson)
intro: An animated lesson about how your spine works, what poor posture does to your body, and the simple changes that help. Listen for the numbers and the practical tips.
summary: Posture is the position in which we hold our bodies when we sit or stand, and it affects how well the body copes with stresses such as carrying loads, awkward positions and gravity. Seen from behind, the 33 vertebrae of a healthy spine form a straight column; from the side, the spine has three natural curves that help absorb shock. Babies are born with a single C-shaped curve, and the other curves develop at around 12 to 18 months. Poor posture makes some muscles tight and overworked while others weaken, adds wear to joints and ligaments, can make the lungs less efficient, and is linked to back pain and tension headaches. Computers, phones and long hours of sitting are making posture worse. The video recommends keeping the neck upright, shoulders relaxed, knees at a right angle and feet flat; a screen at or just below eye level; support for the elbows and wrists; a headset for calls; sleeping on your side with a pillow between the knees; low-heeled shoes; and carrying loads close to the body with a backpack worn evenly. Above all, staying still for long periods is harmful even with good posture, so we should move often, exercise and see a physical therapist if we are worried.

vocab.m: the position in which you hold your body when you sit or stand
the small bones that form the spine (singular: vertebra)
to take in the force of a hit or a jump so it does less damage
a strong band of tissue that holds bones together at a joint
designed to be comfortable and safe for the body to use
the way parts are arranged in a straight or correct line

levels.title: Let's Learn English Level 2 Lesson 3: He Said - She Said
levels.speaker: Anna, Pete and Kelly
levels.intro: Anna and Pete are very late for a meeting with Kelly, their director. Each of them tells a different story about what happened. Listen for the past perfect: had + past participle.
levels.summary: Anna and Pete arrive at a meeting with their director, Kelly, 43 minutes late, and Kelly asks what happened. They had agreed to meet at 8:00 and go to work together. In Anna's story, Pete stopped for his special coffee and she waited about 15 minutes. She also says she left Kelly a message, but Kelly did not get it. In Pete's story, he arrived on time but Anna was hugging a tree; then she wanted to ride scooters, which Pete did not like, and she stopped at a pond to feed birds that she had named after characters from books, such as Romeo, Juliet and Sherlock. Kelly sees that they tell the same event in very different ways and suggests a new show called He Said, She Said, where each person gives their own point of view. The lesson teaches the past perfect and reminds viewers that in the United States people should be on time for business meetings or call to explain.

levels.title: Secrets of success in 8 words, 3 minutes
levels.speaker: Richard St. John
levels.intro: A teenager on a plane asked Richard St. John a simple question: what leads to success? He spent seven years finding the answer. Listen for the eight one-word secrets.
levels.summary: On a plane to the TED conference, a teenage girl from a poor family asked Richard St. John what leads to success, and he did not have a good answer. So, over seven years, he interviewed about 500 successful people at TED and turned their answers into eight words. Passion: they do it for love, not money, and the money often follows. Work: success is hard work, but they enjoy it, so he calls them work-a-frolics, not workaholics. Good: you have to practise and get really good at something. Focus: concentrate on one thing. Push: push yourself through shyness and self-doubt; the architect Frank Gehry said his mother pushed him. Serve: give other people something of value, because that is how people really get rich. Ideas: good ideas, such as Bill Gates's idea for a software company, come from doing simple things. Persist: keep going through failure, criticism and rejection. He jokes that the easy answer is to pay to go to TED, and if not, to do the eight things.

to give all your attention to one thing

to continue trying even when it is difficult

levels.title: The happy secret to better work
levels.speaker: Shawn Achor
levels.intro: A fast, very funny talk by a Harvard-trained psychologist who argues that we have the link between happiness and success the wrong way round. Listen for the statistics and the 21-day plan.
levels.summary: Shawn Achor opens with a childhood story: when his five-year-old sister fell off a bunk bed, he stopped her crying by telling her that the way she had landed proved she was a unicorn. He argues that researchers usually delete the outliers to get a clean trend line, so science learns how to be average instead of studying the people who are far above the curve. After many years at Harvard he noticed that students quickly stopped feeling lucky and focused on competition, workload and stress. He claims that only about 10% of long-term happiness is predicted by external circumstances, and that IQ predicts only about 25% of job success; the other 75% depends on optimism, social support and seeing stress as a challenge rather than a threat. He jokes that a school's 'wellness week' about depression, drugs and violence was really a sickness week. The common formula - work harder, succeed, then be happy - is backwards, he says, because every success moves the goalposts, and because a positive brain works better: it is 31% more productive, 37% better at sales, and doctors in a positive mood make correct diagnoses 19% faster. Dopamine also switches on the brain's learning centres. Finally, he says the brain can be retrained in 21 days by writing down three new things you are grateful for each day, journaling about one positive experience, exercising, meditating and doing random acts of kindness.

to change the target just as you are about to reach it
the way one action spreads and causes more effects, like circles in water

syn.model: Shawn Achor contends that most schools and companies have the formula for success the wrong way round. We assume that if we work harder we will succeed, and that success will then make us happy. Yet every achievement simply raises the bar, so happiness is pushed ever further into the future. Drawing on his research, he shows that an optimistic brain functions more effectively: people in a good mood are 31 per cent more productive, sell 37 per cent more, and doctors reach correct diagnoses 19 per cent faster. Because only a quarter of job success is predicted by IQ, he suggests training the mind instead. Simple routines repeated for 21 days, such as noting three things we are grateful for, exercising, meditating and doing small acts of kindness, can rewire the brain and spread waves of optimism through a whole organisation.

rep.title: Formal account in reported speech
rep.prompt: Write a formal account of Achor's talk for a staff training newsletter (110–150 words), in reported speech. Use at least three different reporting verbs and no contractions.
rep.model: Shawn Achor began by describing how, as a child, he had persuaded his younger sister that her fall from a bunk bed proved she was a unicorn. He argued that researchers too often removed the outliers from their data and therefore learned only how to be average. He pointed out that external circumstances predicted only about ten per cent of long-term happiness, while IQ accounted for just a quarter of job success. He contended that the usual formula, in which success came first and happiness later, was backwards, because every achievement raised the bar. He stressed that a brain in a positive state was 31 per cent more productive. Finally, he proposed that people could retrain their brains within 21 days through gratitude, journaling, exercise, meditation and acts of kindness.

arg.title: Argue a position
arg.prompt: 'Companies should make their employees happier before they ask them to work harder.' Write a formal argument (150–200 words). Use ideas from the talk, present the other side, and give your own view. No contractions.
starters: However, critics would point out that …
arg.model: Shawn Achor argues that happiness is not the reward for success but the engine that drives it. According to his research, employees in a positive state are about 31 per cent more productive and considerably better at sales. Moreover, a workplace that values gratitude, exercise and small acts of kindness may also reduce stress and staff turnover, which are expensive problems for any company. Therefore, investing in well-being could be a sound business decision rather than a luxury. However, critics would point out that happiness cannot simply be ordered from above. Some well-being programmes feel artificial, and employees may resent being told to smile while their workload remains unbearable. Furthermore, a company that neglects clear goals and fair pay will not be rescued by meditation sessions. In my view, the two aims are not in conflict. Firms should certainly create conditions in which people can thrive, such as reasonable hours, supportive managers and recognition for good work. Nevertheless, these efforts should accompany, not replace, honest expectations. When employees feel valued, demanding high standards becomes far easier to justify.

levels.title: The power of introverts
levels.speaker: Susan Cain
levels.intro: A gentle, witty and carefully argued talk about why schools and workplaces undervalue quiet people. Listen for her distinction between introversion and shyness and for her three calls to action.
levels.summary: Susan Cain recalls going to summer camp at the age of nine with a suitcase full of books, because reading together was what her family did; at camp she was pressed to be loud and outgoing, so the books stayed under her bed. She later became a Wall Street lawyer instead of the writer she wanted to be, partly to prove she could be bold. She explains that introversion concerns how people respond to stimulation, and that it is different from shyness, which is a fear of social judgement. Between a third and a half of people are introverts, yet classrooms have moved to group work in pods and offices to open-plan layouts, and teachers often prefer extroverted pupils. Research by Adam Grant at Wharton found that introverted leaders often get better results with proactive employees, because they let them run with their ideas, and figures such as Eleanor Roosevelt, Rosa Parks and Gandhi described themselves as quiet or shy. She argues that solitude is often key to creativity: Darwin took long walks alone, Dr Seuss worked alone in a private studio, and Steve Wozniak built the first Apple computer working on his own. She describes a historical shift from a culture of character to a culture of personality that prizes charisma and salesmanship. She remembers her grandfather, a modest rabbi who preached for 62 years and whose funeral filled the streets of his neighbourhood. She ends with three calls to action: stop the madness for constant group work, take time to step away and reflect, and look at what is inside your own suitcase and share it - and she wishes the audience the courage to speak softly.

syn.text: Cain [argues] that modern schools and offices [favour] [loud] personalities. She [believes] that [quiet] people [contribute] a great deal when they are given space.
syn.model: In this eloquent and gently subversive talk, Susan Cain contends that contemporary classrooms and workplaces are biased towards gregarious personalities, treating the capacity to speak up as though it were synonymous with the capacity to think well. Drawing on her childhood memory of a suitcase of books that never left its hiding place at summer camp, she distinguishes introversion, a matter of how much stimulation we can comfortably absorb, from shyness, which is rooted in a fear of judgement. Since between a third and a half of the population are introverted, she is convinced that our obsession with open-plan offices and relentless group work squanders an enormous reservoir of talent. Reserved individuals, she insists, often lead proactive teams more effectively and offer original ideas precisely because solitude allows them to reflect. Her plea is not for the abolition of teamwork but for a culture that grants people the privacy and autonomy in which their best thinking can flourish.

rep.prompt: Write a formal account of Cain's talk for a university magazine (130–170 words), in reported speech. Use at least three different reporting verbs and no contractions.
rep.model: Susan Cain opened by recalling that, at the age of nine, she had taken a suitcase full of books to summer camp, only to be told that she should be more outgoing. She confessed that she had later become a Wall Street lawyer partly to prove that she could be bold. She contended that introversion concerned the way in which people responded to stimulation and insisted that it should not be confused with shyness, which she described as a fear of social judgement. She observed that between a third and a half of the population were introverts, yet she warned that schools and workplaces were increasingly designed for extroverts. Citing research by Adam Grant, she asserted that introverted leaders often achieved better results with proactive employees. She concluded by urging her audience to stop the constant drive for group work and to share what was in their own suitcases.

arg.title: Argue a position
arg.prompt: 'Schools should spend less time on group work and more time on independent study.' Write a formal argument (200–260 words). Use ideas from the talk, present the other side, and give your own view. No contractions.
starters: Nevertheless, it could be argued that …
arg.model: Susan Cain maintains that our schools have become structured around the needs of extroverts, with desks pushed into pods and even solitary disciplines such as creative writing turned into committee work. It is undeniable that this trend carries real costs. Between a third and a half of pupils are introverts, and many of them do their deepest thinking alone; moreover, solitude has historically nourished remarkable creativity, from Darwin's long walks to Wozniak's late nights at the workbench. A classroom that constantly demands collaboration may therefore reward the most talkative pupils rather than the most thoughtful ones. Nevertheless, it could be argued that group work prepares young people for a world in which almost every profession depends on cooperation. Pupils need to learn how to negotiate, to listen and to disagree constructively, and these skills cannot be acquired in isolation. Furthermore, for some children, structured teamwork is the only setting in which they are encouraged to speak at all. I would argue that the real problem is not group work itself but its indiscriminate use. Teachers should alternate deliberately between the two modes, allowing pupils to think independently before they pool their ideas, so that the reflective child arrives at the discussion with something to say. Consequently, the question is not whether pupils should work together or alone, but how a school can protect the hour of solitary thought on which good collaboration ultimately depends.
